Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Michael is a 28-year-old financial analyst who came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he would not have admitted he needed help. The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. His two-year-old daughter, Ella, developed a high fever that turned into bacterial meningitis within hours. He remembers every detail of that night: the humid August air pressing against the windows, the way the streetlights reflected off the wet pavement after a sudden thunderstorm, the frantic drive to the emergency room. What he cannot seem to hold onto is the moment the doctor told them she might not make it. Every time he tries to bring that memory fully into his mind, something slams shut—he pushes it away before the complete picture forms. What remains are fragments: the beeping monitors, his wife’s hand gripping his arm, the pale blue of Ella’s hospital gown. Those images are permanently vivid, playing back like a short film he cannot turn off.

In the months since Ella recovered fully, Michael has not recovered. He works in a high-rise office where his desk faces a window, and he now finds himself scanning the floor plan for exits before he can sit down. He tells himself it is just being prepared, but he knows it is more than that. On rainy days—especially warm, humid ones that remind him of that August night—he cannot focus at all. The weather makes his chest tighten, and he spends the day checking the news, searching for anything about pediatric illnesses or hospital outbreaks, as if the danger is still coming for his daughter. He has started leaving meetings early if a colleague mentions a sick child, and he has stopped attending any social events where children might be present. His wife’s sister invited them to her son’s birthday party last month, and Michael found a dozen reasons not to go. The real reason was simple: being around children made him feel like something terrible was about to happen.

At night, the vigilance does not stop. He cannot fall asleep because he needs to stay alert, listening for any sound from Ella’s room, or for sirens outside, or for the smell of fever. He often jolts awake certain that something is wrong, even when the house is quiet and his daughter is sleeping peacefully. He has come to believe that he is no longer the person he used to be. That old self—the confident analyst who could read a spreadsheet and plan for any market shift—feels gone. In his place is someone who flinches at a child’s cough, who scans every room for danger, who still hears himself whispering “I should have protected her” even though the doctors said he did everything right. He knows, logically, that he could not have prevented meningitis. But the thought sits beneath everything: he failed. He was supposed to keep her safe, and he did not.

His job has suffered. He has missed deadlines because he cannot stop searching the news for related stories. His boss has noticed his distraction, and Michael fears he will be passed over for a promotion he had been working toward for years. His marriage is strained; his wife has told him he is not the same man she married, and he knows she is right. He avoids talking about the hospital stay, and when she tries to bring it up, he shuts down. He feels unrecognizable to himself, and that may be the most frightening part.

What finally brought Michael to therapy was an episode last week. He was driving home on a rainy evening, and a news alert about a local pediatric illness flashed on his phone. He nearly swerved off the road. His heart pounded so hard he had to pull over, convinced for a moment that the danger was happening again, right then. He sat in the car for twenty minutes, planning an escape route from the highway, before he could drive the remaining mile home. That night, he told his wife he would get help. He does not know what he hopes for exactly—maybe to sleep through the night, maybe to stop flinching at his own daughter’s laughter—but he is terrified that if he does not change, he will lose everything he still has.
